introduction

What happens when a crisis hits?

Crises change how we think about mobility.

Everyday patterns break down, and new kinds of movement appear:

  • evacuations
  • responders and aid workers arriving
  • people who leave and later return

The data gaps

What are the data gaps ?

Timeliness and continuity

How quickly can crisis-induced mobility be detected, and can it be monitored consistently over time?

Spatial granularity

Where are people displaced from and to, including within cities and across administrative boundaries?

Mobility dynamics and trajectories

When do people leave, how often do they move, and when or where do they return?

Demographic and socioeconomic disaggregation

Who leaves, who stays, and how do vulnerabilities interact with crises ?

Duration, persistence and recovery

How long does the effects of crisis persist?

Part 1 · Internal displacement

Displacement detection on CDR

Home location approach

The usual view in mobile phone data studies: find each person's home before and after the disaster. A different home means displaced.

Activity space approach

Instead of one point, map every place a person spends time in before the disaster, and which of these places they sleep in.

Loss of habitual spaces

After the disaster, check every day whether the person is still in a familiar place. A sustained stay in places never visited before is displacement.

The contribution

Conceptual mapping, and detailed mapping of each move.

Challenges

Biases and challenges of MPD

Sensitive

Raw records reveal a life: home, work, health, faith. Processing must be privacy-aware before anything else.

Not everyone

SIMs are not people: children out; elderly, women and other operators' customers under-seen.

The crisis bends the data

Damaged towers and dead batteries go silent. Silence is not absence.

Hard to check

Sources differ in time, space and definition. No ground truth during a crisis.

Hard to access

Five ways to share mobile phone data. Each has its own issue.
